﴿When the sky is split open,﴾ ﴿and it hearkens to its Lord and it is right that it should;﴾ ﴿and when the earth is stretched out,﴾ ﴿and casts out what is in it and empties itself,﴾ ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and it is right that it should;﴾ ﴿O humankind, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him.﴾ ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand,﴾ ﴿he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾ ﴿and will return to his people joyful.﴾ ﴿But as for him who is given his record behind his back,﴾ ﴿he will call for destruction﴾ ﴿and will burn in the Blaze.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he used to be joyful among his people.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he thought he would never return.﴾ ﴿Yes! Indeed, his Lord has been ever-Seeing of him.﴾

These are descriptions of the Day of Resurrection. "The splitting of the sky" (inshiqaq al-sama') is its breaking apart out of the terror of the Day of Resurrection, as God the Exalted says: ﴿And the sky will be split open, for on that Day it will be frail﴾ [al-Haqqah: 16]. Al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and others said: it is its being cracked by clouds. Some people said: its cracking is its opening up into gates for the descent and ascent of the angels in the terror of the Day of Resurrection.

Abu 'Amr read "inshaqqat" and paused on the taʾ as if he were sounding a trace of the genitive vowel (kasra) on it, and likewise in its counterparts. Abu Hatim said: I heard an eloquent Bedouin in the lands of Qays pronounce these ta's with a kasra, and this is a dialect.

The word "adhinat" means: it listened and heard His command and prohibition. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "God has never listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an beautifully." From this also is the verse of the poet: (p-568)

Deaf when they hear good said of me,
but when you are mentioned with evil in their presence, they listen.

As for God the Exalted's words "and it is right (huqqat)," Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jubayr said its meaning is: it is right for it to hear and obey. It may also be meant: it is right for it to split apart because of the intensity of the terror and the fear of God the Exalted.

The "stretching out of the earth" (madd al-ard) is the removal of its mountains, so that no crookedness or hillock remains in it. That is its stretching. In a hadith: "God the Exalted will stretch out the earth on the Day of Resurrection like a leather hide of 'Ukaz."

"And it casts out what is in it" means: the dead. This is what the majority said. Al-Zajjaj said: it means treasures. But this is weak, because that happens at the time of the emergence of the Dajjal, whereas on the Day of Resurrection it is only the dead that are cast out.

"And empties itself" (takhallat) means: it became empty of what was in it, that is, it held onto nothing of them.

God the Exalted's words ﴿O humankind﴾ address the human species as a whole. "Al-kadih" is one who works with intensity, speed and striving that leaves its mark. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever asks while he has enough to suffice him, his request will come on the Day of Resurrection as a bruise or a scratch on his face." The meaning is: you are doing good or evil, and you will inevitably be journeying toward your Lord, because time flies with the lifespan of a human being; his lifespan is only a period of swift travel toward his Lord. This is a verse of admonition and reminder, that is: be wary of this condition, and do righteous deeds, which you will find.

Talha read the idgham (assimilation) of the kaf of "innaka" into the kaf of "kadih." From this word is the verse of the poet: (p-569)

What is a human being but one deluded,
toiling all his days in a low state.

Qatada said: whoever is able to make his toil in obedience to God, let him do so. God the Exalted's words ﴿and you will meet Him﴾ mean: you will meet His punishment or His bliss.

The grammarians differed about the governing element (al-'amil) of "idha" (when). Some grammarians said the governing element is "inshaqqat." Many of their leading scholars rejected this, because "idha" is in construct with "inshaqqat," and whoever permits this weakens the construct relation in their view and strengthens the sense of the conditional.

Others among them said the governing element is "fa-mulaqihi (you will meet Him)." Some of their skilled scholars said the governing element is a hidden verb. They likewise differed about the response (jawab) of "idha." Many grammarians said it is omitted because the listener already knows it. Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash said it is in God the Exalted's words ﴿O humankind, you are toiling toward your Lord with toil, and you will meet Him﴾, meaning: when the sky is split open, then you will meet God the Exalted. It was also said the estimated reading is "fa-ya ayyuha al-insan," and the response of "idha" is in the estimated fa'. Al-Farra' said, on behalf of some grammarians, that it is "adhinat" with an added estimated waw.

As for the pronoun in "fa-mulaqihi," the majority of commentators said it refers to the Lord the Exalted, so the fa' here is coordinating "mulaq" with "kadih." Some people said it refers to the toil (kadh), so the fa' here is coordinating a sentence with the one before it, and the estimate is: "then you will meet it," and the meaning is: you will meet its recompense, good or evil.

Then God divided people into believer and disbeliever. The believers are given their records in their right hands. As for those among the disobedient upon whom the threat is carried out, they are given their record when they come out of the Fire. Some people permitted that they be given it first, before entering the Fire, and this verse refutes that view. The "easy reckoning" is the presentation (al-'ard). As for one whose reckoning is subjected to scrutiny (nuqisha al-hisab), he will perish and be punished. Likewise the Messenger of God ﷺ said to 'A'isha (p-570) may God be pleased with her, when he said: "Whoever is reckoned will be punished." 'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, said: Has not God said: ﴿he will be reckoned with an easy reckoning﴾, and so on? He, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "That is only the presentation. As for one whose reckoning is scrutinized, he will perish."

In a hadith through Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "God the Exalted will bring the servant near until He places His screen (kanaf) over him, and says: Did I not do such-and-such for you? He enumerates his blessings. Then He says: Why did you do such-and-such, for His sins? So the servant stands in disgrace, and God the Exalted says: I concealed it from you in the world, and I forgive it for you today."

'A'isha, may God be pleased with her, said: I heard the Prophet ﷺ say: "O God, reckon with me with an easy reckoning." I said: O Messenger of God, and what is that? He said: "That He overlooks the evil deeds."

Ibn 'Umar narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever holds himself to account in this world, God the Exalted will make his reckoning light on the Day of Resurrection."

God the Exalted's words ﴿to his people﴾ mean those whom God the Exalted has prepared for him in Paradise, whether from the women of this world, or from the dark-eyed houris, or from all of them.

(p-571) The disbeliever is given his record from behind him, because his hands are shackled. It is related that his hand will be inserted into his chest until it comes out from behind his back, and he takes his record with it.

It is said that these two verses were revealed concerning Abu Salama ibn 'Abd al-Asad and his brother al-Aswad. Abu Salama was among the best of the Muslims, and his brother was among the stubborn disbelievers.

"Yad'u thubura" means: he cries out lamenting, "Woe to me! Alas for my grief!" and similar words whose meaning is: this is your time and your moment, that is, come to me. Thubur is a comprehensive term for calamities, like "wayl" (woe).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Kisa'i, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, al-Jahdari, Abu al-Sha'tha' and al-A'raj read ﴿wa-yusla﴾ with a shaddah on the lam and a damma on the ya', for emphasis. Nafi' also read, and 'Asim in the narration of Aban, with a damma on the ya' and a lightened lam; this is the reading of Abu al-Ashhab, 'Isa, and Harun from Abu 'Amr. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamza, Abu Ja'far, Qatada, 'Isa, Talha and al-A'mash read with a fatha on the ya', on the active verb form. In the Mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud it is "wa-sa-yusla." God the Exalted's words ﴿among his people﴾ mean in the world, that is, that possession of that (joy) knows only joy with his people without knowledge of God the Exalted. If a believer is happy with his people, there is no fault upon him.

God the Exalted's words ﴿Indeed, he thought he would never return﴾ mean: he would never return to God the Exalted to be raised and gathered. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: I did not know the meaning of "yahur" until I heard a Bedouin woman say to a little girl of hers: "Hurry back (huri)," that is, return. The verb "thanna" here retains its original sense, and "anna" and what follows it fill the place of the two objects of "thanna." It is the lightened form of "anna" (that), and "al-hawar" is returning by the same path. From this is the saying: "O God, I seek refuge in You from hawar after kawar." (p-572)

Then God the Exalted refuted the disbeliever's supposition with His words, glorified be He: ﴿Yes!﴾, that is: he will return and come back. Then He informed them that God the Exalted has always been Seeing of them, nothing of anyone's deeds being hidden from Him. In this is a warning.

The Quranic verses are given first, with their meanings in the markers:

﴿So I swear by the twilight﴾ ﴿and the night and what it gathers﴾ ﴿and the moon when it becomes full﴾ ﴿You will surely ride through stage after stage﴾ ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾ ﴿And when the Quran is recited to them, they do not prostrate﴾ ﴿Rather, those who disbelieve deny it﴾ ﴿And Allah knows best what they conceal﴾ ﴿So give them the good news of a painful punishment﴾ ﴿Except those who believe and do righteous deeds; for them is a reward never cut off﴾

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary:

"Lā" is an extra particle (zā'idah), and the sense is: "fa-uqsimu" (so I swear). It was also said that "lā" refutes the statements of the disbelievers, and then the speech begins with "uqsimu" (I swear). Allah's swearing by His creatures is for the sake of honouring them and drawing attention to them for the lesson they contain, since swearing by them is a reminder from them.

"Al-shafaq" is the redness that follows the setting of the sun, together with the whiteness that generally accompanies it. It was also said that al-shafaq here means the whole day; this was reported from Mujahid, but it is a weak view. Abu Hurayra and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: al-shafaq is the whiteness that is followed by the redness.

"Wasaqa" means to gather and bring together, and from it comes "al-wasq", meaning a gathered load of sā' measures. The night gathers all living creatures together, that is, it collects them within itself and draws them in. Likewise, all creatures on the earth and in the air, including the seas, the mountains, the winds and other things, are gathered in it.

"Ittisāq al-qamar" means the moon's completion and perfection when it becomes full (badr), so the meaning is that it became filled with light.

Nāfi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Āmir, 'Āṣim, Ibn 'Abbās (according to one of the two transmissions from him), Abu Ja'far, al-Ḥasan, al-A'mash, Qatāda and Ibn Jubayr read "latarkabunna" with a damma on the bā', addressing the people. The meaning is: you will surely ride the hardships, death, resurrection and reckoning, state after state. Or the states may be from the sperm-drop to old age, just as one says "ṭabaqah ba'da ṭabaqah" (one stratum after another). "'An" may come in the sense of "ba'd" (after), as one says: "waritha al-majda kābiran 'an kābir" (he inherited glory, elder after elder). It was also said that the meaning is: you will surely ride these states, nation after nation. From this is the saying of al-'Abbās ibn 'Abd al-Muṭṭalib, may Allah be pleased with him, about the Prophet (ﷺ):

"You, when you were sent, the earth was illuminated, and the paths shone with your light.
You are transferred from loin to womb; when one age passes, another stratum appears."

That is, a generation of people, because it is a layer (ṭabaq) of the earth. Al-Aqra' ibn Ḥābis said:

"I am a man who has milked the age to its dregs, and a stratum of it has driven me from one stratum to another."

That is, state after state. It was also said that the meaning is: you will surely ride the Hereafter after the first life. 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, read "layarkabunna", treating them in the third person. Abu 'Ubayda said the meaning is: you will surely ride the ways of those before you.

The qāḍī Abu Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Just as in the (prophetic) ḥadīth: "a span for a span, and a cubit for a cubit." This is "ṭabaq 'an ṭabaq". This meaning fits with the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb that we mentioned, and it is also suitable with the first reading.

Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī, 'Amr ibn Mas'ūd, Ibn 'Abbās, Mujahid, al-Aswad, Ibn Jubayr, Ma'rūf, al-Sha'bī, Abu al-'Āliya, Ibn Thābit and 'Īsā read "latarkabanna" with a fatḥah on the bā', meaning: you, O Muhammad. It was said the meaning is: state after state, from the struggle with the disbelievers. Ibn 'Abbās said: heaven after heaven during the Night Journey. It was also said that it is a promise of victory, meaning: you will surely ride the affair of the Arabs tribe after tribe and conquest after conquest, as happened and was found after that. Ibn Mas'ūd said the meaning is: you (or the heaven) will surely ride through the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, state after state, when it becomes like molten brass and like oil-dregs, and it splits and cracks. In this reading the heaven is the doer. Ibn 'Abbās and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, also read "layarkabanna" in the third person. This may refer to Muhammad (ﷺ) according to the meanings mentioned earlier. Ibn 'Abbās also said it means your Prophet (ﷺ) as a leader. Some people, in the book of al-Naqqāsh, said the intended subject is the moon, because it changes in states, phases and beginnings of months.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, addressed His Prophet (ﷺ), while the intended audience is those disbelievers, with His words: ﴿So what is wrong with them that they do not believe?﴾, meaning: what argument do they have against these clear proofs? The majority read "yukadhdhibūna" with a ḍamma on the yā' and a shaddah on the dhāl. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk read it with a fatḥah on the yā', a lightened dhāl and a sukūn on the kāf. "Yū'ūna" means they gather from deeds, denial and disbelief, as if they put them into containers. You say: "wa'aytu al-'ilm" (I preserved knowledge) and "awa'aytu al-matā'" (I stored the goods). Allah, may He be exalted, made the good news to be of punishment, because He stated it explicitly; when good news comes unrestricted, it is only of goodness.

Then Allah, may He be exalted, made an exception from the disbelievers of Quraysh: the people for whom faith had already been decreed in His decree. "Mamnūn" means cut off, from their saying: "ḥablun manīn" (a severed rope). From this is the saying of al-Ḥārith ibn Ḥillizah al-Yashkurī:

"You see behind them, from the dust and the gathering, cut-off swirls, as if they were scattered particles."

He means broken, scattered dust. Ibn 'Abbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "mamnūn" means counted against them, reckoned, and spoiled by reproach.

The commentary on Surat al-Inshiqāq is complete, and all praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
